title: Justin Andrew Miclat and Andy Day

sentences.text: Steve, how you doing?
This meeting is being recorded.
Morning sir, how you doing?
Doing well.
Good, good.
Whereabouts you guys calling from?
I am based in Las Vegas and Steve is based in Los Angeles.
What about yourself?
I'm in the UK so just, just about an hour outside of London.
But I did live in Los Angeles in 23 for, for six months.
So quite, quite familiar with Los Angeles.
At least you escaped.
I'm happy for you.
Had a pretty short ski.
Well, it depends.
It's worse here.
I think it's on a scale.
England's somewhere over here, maybe America's somewhere over there, I don't know.
But I would rather be over there than that way.
Is that right?
Interesting.
Yeah.
But the good thing is it's hot here today and it's been really hot for a while but usually it just rains and it's dark, so.
Yeah, no, I hear you.
I did, I went out there maybe a year and a half ago.
We had a client producing a documentary so was there for a couple days, did a couple touristy things in and out so maybe didn't get the best view.
The country hopefully can, can pop back out there soon enough.
Yeah, it's, well it's, it's good for tour tourist attractions, London in particular.
So it's not all bad.
But yeah, you can't be Vegas.
I guess it's going to be the best.
Vegas is fun.
It's been been a couple of years now that I got out of la.
Still have family and friends there but initially came here for work which I'm sure we'll get into in a bit.
But some of the agency work that we started to do with and for our clients, somebody had come here to Nevada and I haven't left since pretty much.
Brilliant, brilliant.
Well, must be hot there.
But anyway, good to see you guys and thank you for booking the call.
So usually these calls are a tear down call.

So the, the process usually is, you know, we kind of get into the business how you're running it and what the kind of issues are that you're hitting, if any and what your strategy is, what your plan is, what your ultimate goal is and then we can work through the low hanging fruit and also a sort of, you know, bigger strategy maybe that would help you towards an exit of some kind.
But I'm happy for you guys to sort of guide that depending on what it is that you're looking for.
I can see in the questionnaire that you put that you were looking to position the company to create new monetization channels and have access to global sponsorship networks.
But I would love to hear from you guys what it is that you do.
Just to give you a bit of background about us, we are capital A group, so we're an M and A advisory in marketing services.
So our clients are marketing services buyers or sellers.
So that would be marketing agencies.
And the buyers tend to be either high growth agencies or they can be investment companies, sometimes private investment, but otherwise private equity investors.
Where they've acquired a company, we help them to target businesses to acquire so they can grow through that.
But we also have agencies co, which is our marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell agency businesses.
So.
But let me give you the mic and you tell me what's going on in your business and what you're hoping to get from the call.
Sure.
No, I appreciate the introduction and thank you for your time.
I'll give you the high level and we can talk more granular specificity as needed.
But Steve and I co founded the company seven years ago, August of 20 what?
2018, I think it was 2018.
I come from a background of a combination of legal training, so I have a law degree and I worked in sports and sports management and partnerships.
Right.
And so right around the time of the company's inception is when there was getting to be a lot of buzz around the intersection of marketing partnerships.

Some of the athletes that I had worked with and been around and gaming and live streaming and Twitch, if you're not familiar, Twitch is a platform where a lot of that entertainment focused video game content lives and is consumed daily.
And so I founded a company to service more specifically those streamers and content creators and channels tailored to and focused on games and video game content.
And so 2018, 2019, early days, a lot of it was still starting to bubble.

But as you may have already seen in documents that Steve has put together, who oversees our finance and operations and things really started to pick up relatively significantly 2021, 2022, where we've had consistent eight figure years in revenue and sales, combination of brand partnerships, media rights deals, merch, licensing, et cetera.
But as you probably know at this point, given your background in M and A, as all things do in entertainment, it's all cyclical, right?

And so we've seen over the past couple of years the inevitable kind of deflation of that bubble downturn, which by and large we've been able to endure through a handful of pretty sizable partnership deals and some pretty reputable clients who still brought in consistent deal flow.

We've countered some of that downswing by being a little bit more aggressive this past year in terms of hiring, in terms of signing new clientele, in terms of reimagining how we work with talent clients and positioning us to partner with them to build new monetization opportunities and revenue streams.

But at the same token, and with the team that we currently have, a team of eight, I'm wanting and we're willing to more aggressively explore what an acquisition or an investment looks like so that we can continue to grow and build and sustain the services that we offer to our clients and then some.
I'm trying my hardest not to use the word scale the business.
Right.
Because I don't know necessarily if that's kind of what I'm looking for or what I want.
Right.
I think more than anything else is I want to make sure that I equip my team and my clients clients with an abundance of the highest quality resources, opportunities and information.
It need not be an outfit that manages 80 creators.
It could be around the same scale and size that we have right now, which is in that 15 to 30 clientele mark.
So long as we're doing a lot of great work and generating a lot of money.
So that's kind of where we're at.
We've explored or been approached with a handful of acquisition opportunities over the past couple years.
Had a lot of interest during the pandemic when gaming and live streaming and that culture really started to pick up.
For better or worse, we explored them and had those conversations, but held out to continue to chip away at what we were doing independently.
And that kind of leads us to where we're at right now, where I, at least, and personally I know Steve as well, is as motivated as ever to, to find the right potential partners to.
To continue to work in the space.
Okay, brilliant.
Well, thank you for that.
So.
So around 21 to 22, you got up to eight figures.
Have you sustained that?
Whereabouts is the the business?
Sort of the last two years and currently I'm just looking at our overview right now.
What 23 gross revenue 4.4 24 gross avenue 3.3, 25 year to date 315k.
So we've seen significant drops in the gross revenue side of things.
And on the sales side.
Right.
Gross sales 23 is 21 million, 24 is 14 million.
25 year to date is 2.5 million.
So we've been buoyed by a particular type of spending on the media, Right.
Side of things for our agency and the channels that we manage.
And thankfully.
Right.
We were relatively conservative with our spending so that we have this kind of buffer now to be able to endure and survive some of this, the downswing of things.
So, you know, like I said, and Steve and I are aligned on our belief and assessment in knowing the.
The space and entertainment industry as a whole that it may not rise back again to that 22, 2015, 18 gross sales mark, but that we're kind of in that downswing now that it should uptick.
And I feel like in some ways there might be a buyer who similarly sees that opportunity and philosophy and might want to work with us because of our experience through those ebbs and flows.
Yeah, Carl, that's tough, isn't it?
It's a tough story.
It's been good.
It's been good.
First time entrepreneur and really got into it with no real expectation or desire to exit.
Right.
You see the window of where there's clients and a service of opportunity and need in an emerging market and you dive in.
So it's been good in a lot of ways.
So how did you get stuck there?
Because you guys were clearly innovators.
I don't know whether you're gamers naturally.
Is that like your.
Your thing or did you just get into it as you.
Were you.
Not really.
I think we both played video games growing up.
I don't think either of us are.

I know I'm not personally playing video games daily where we're both parents, we're both fathers and so gaming and video game culture has definitely been siloed to the work part of it, I think in a lot of ways.
To answer your question, taking learnings from our respective experiences and client services in entertainment, mine from sports and working with athletes.
Steve's in servicing artists, musicians and celebrities on the finance side of things and kind of bringing all those elements together to service this particular type of clientele has allowed us to.
To gain that trust and have that success that we've had historically.
Yeah, but you've done so well.
I mean, you've done so well previously.
Thanks.
And so that, that when the, when it started declining, what.
What has stopped you switching to a different track away from gaming?
Because I mean, it strikes me you could jump into sports and music and other genres to sort of pick things up.
But.
But has that not been forthcoming or you just haven't tried it or.

The thing that appealed to myself and I believe speak on behalf of Steve in this respect as well, appealed to us back when we started the company is how nascent the clientele or at least the mainstream Appeal and commercial ability of this clientele is or was, and now even still is, five, six, seven years later.
I'm a big sports fan.
Steve is a big sports fan.
We, we enjoy it, we consume it, but at the same time, especially as someone who's personally worked in sports, I don't care to work in that space.
Right.
It's.

It's a very understood and mature marketplace and business model that doesn't afford a lot of innovation or creativity in the same way comparatively that gaming, live streaming, Twitch and this type of clientele does.
So in a lot of ways, we've been told and have had conversations where it's the wild, wild west.
And it's true, it at least has been.
And I think that's what has afforded us a lot of success early days is being able to be innovative and imagine certain possibilities for revenue generation and commercialization.
And I think a lot of that now has become more acceptable practice and it's become much more competitive and saturated space.
Hence, kind of how we've now been one of many outfits within the market.
Yeah, but your skill set is, is around, I guess, the monetization of the creators and those creators really could come from multiple genres, I'm thinking.
So that's, that's why I'm interested in.
Yeah, no, it's going to other, other verticals.
It's true, it's true.
And you know, I'll say to that end, we've diversified the verticals and audiences that our clientele specializes in and speaks to to a certain extent over the years.
I would say that our clientele.
So we have a talent roster of 23 clients.
Right.
Who have a reach of about 50 million across all of their platforms.
All of them have some foundation, some basis in video games gaming content.
And I guess the underlying sentiment is competition.
Right.
We look to bring on clientele that competes in some way, shape or form through their content and through their business.
You know, kind of our biggest client over the past few years is someone that was a massive sports fan, has as family who's played, you know, professional football, collegiate football.

And so a lot of the revenue opportunities and partnerships we've been able to bring to the table through with and for him were with, you know, the NFL, the ufc, some of these big sports leagues and teams and athletes.
So, you know, we dabbled.

Again, my experience in sports, but back then and even now, present day is frustrating to the extent that they pay you in access to events and, you know, they give you tickets when you produce an event and do something Big we can't pay our bills with tickets.
So I've always enjoyed and appreciated those opportunities of marketing efforts and levers, but never really sought to more fully dive into servicing sports clientele.
Fair enough.
Okay.
Yeah.
So my background is, is, is similar in some ways.
I had a big music website and an entertainment site as well.
But we, we got out of monetization through the music side of things because the music business doesn't, doesn't pay any money to anybody except the top artists.

So, you know, working with brands and it's something that I've always sort of suggested first with clients because of my experience with that, that once you switch the brat to brands and realize that brands have got all the money and it's not, you know, the music companies or the sports companies or whoever else, then it becomes easier to do more.
What would you say is the reason why you've dropped so drastically in revenue?
Clearly there was a massive uptick with people being trapped at home, but 24 people were relatively free to go out and do other things.
But you are only on about a fifth of the revenue for the year or only tracking for a fifth of the revenue, maybe even less.
The largest chunk of sales and revenue opportunities over the past, call it, three years have been media rights deals.
Right?
And so I guess I can summarize the way in which we generate sales and monetize clients in three different ways effectively, right?
Brand partnerships, merchandise and licensing, and media rights.
And so from 22 to 24, we were able to work with a handful of, or a couple, I shouldn't say a handful.
I wish it was a handful, a couple of platforms who acquired the exclusive media rights for our clientele to stream their content on their platforms.
And so that, like I said earlier, that's what buoyed our business, right?
From a brand partnership side, we have generated anywhere between 2 to 4 million in brand partnerships annually.
But then those media rights deals were seven, eight figures.
And so now that there isn't as much competition spending from those platforms, right?
YouTube, Twitch, they're not competing to acquire these exclusive channels or licenses anymore.
That revenue stream has dried up.
Wow.
And so everybody on your roster, all those 23 clients, they're, they're all gamers.
And, and just so I understand it, right, that the majority of the revenue you were getting from them was the meteorite.
So the merch and the brand partnerships, that's, that's never generated the same kind of revenue.
It's never generated the same kind of revenue.
But the majority of the, the Deal flow and the deal volume has come from brand partnerships.
The media rights opportunities were very limited, very exclusive and pertained literally to two clients I think three who we were able to secure six, seven, eight figure deals for.
But from a consistent deal flow perspective, brand partnerships is how we pay our bills and keep the lights on.
So I mean is it quite lumpy then?
And then you've got that revenue coming from through to help with cash flow for the brand partnerships.
But, but you, you've been, you know, going out to dinner on the big meteorites checks that do.
Exactly.
Got it.
And then so the, the brand partnerships work.
That is your bread and butter.
Is that still coming through the business at the same rate?
And this is what it looks like.
Two and a half million or five million for the year.
That is that, that.
No, not at the same, neither at the same time size average deal size nor at the same volume.
And what would you say, why has that changed so drastically?

I think it's really just a matter of brands, advertisers and marketers being really excited about an emerging market and the opportunity to reach that younger audience through a different medium than traditional media and entertainment.
And over the course of time as they've learned how to spend, where to spend, they've decided not to spend.
Right.
Or to spend less because the conversion capabilities or the amount required to invest to see those conversions is a little bit more difficult.
Right.
So I think in a lot of ways, thinking back again to our origin, we were there early days right before money started to trickle into the space significantly.
And now that it has happened, brands are being a lot more thoughtful and strategic about where, how and if they spend money.
Within gaming, there's still a relatively significant amount of money being spent.
And you know, we're still bringing in consistent brand partnerships, but not at the clip that we were in years past.
Right.
So there's, there's two really good skill sets, the meteorites.
And I'm assuming you would, if you had clients in the right space you would still be able to go out and find those deals.
Those big deals are obviously the exciting stuff.
And then potentially yeah, I, I, it's been a combination of, of just the buyers not being there, but also it obviously moved to other trends.
I mean this was clearly a trend that, that ticked up two or three years ago.
But the hockey puck has gone somewhere else.
But you guys have stayed just with the gaming guys.

The streamers when I'm, and I'm just shooting the now so I don't know back but you Know, maybe everybody's moved over, over to, to Tick Tock and so had you moved over to Tick Tock and looked for, you know, trending streamers or whatever you want to call them there.

But if you'd look for those guys and then being, being able to find other channels that you could help them get onto and you could monetize those, like moving them to long form on YouTube and monetizing or some other way of doing the same thing but just with a different vertical.
Do you know what I mean?
That it does.
I do.
And I'll say to a certain extent we have and do service cross pollination onto other platforms like a TikTok in addition to Twitch and YouTube.
It's truly just the case that now the model in which content is consumed and distributed isn't exclusive, right?

Creators, brands, channels are seeing and understanding the value of being on seven platforms all at once and monetizing, maybe in smaller increments, but times seven in part because a, they want to grow and reach as many different audience as possible.
But baby, neither Twitch, nor YouTube nor Kick, right, are paying to exclusively house that content on their own.
It was very clearly an unsustainable, very expensive model for them, the platforms to invest in channels in that way.
Far be it for us to tell them that it was unsustainable.
We were just there to make the most of it, be present and capitalize on their desire to spend.

So, you know, the practice, the skill set in and of itself isn't necessarily affordable from what we've done with twitch into TikTok because TikTok isn't spending or buying the exclusive media rights for content to live on their platform.

It may be the case that a TikTok competitor emerges over the next couple years and then that battle, that competition represents itself in the same way that it did for us in 2223 with Twitch and YouTube.
But that doesn't currently exist in the marketplace.
That makes sense.
It does, yeah, it does.
But I, you know, just very generally I've seen a lot of gamers that have grown on YouTube platforms where they've just got into other kinds of content.
Clearly the gaming staff has a shelf life and they move on to just much more general entertainment content and they've managed to create careers there.

I guess my line of questioning is really because the influencer market is still extremely strong and it does seem like you sit in this lane, a very tight lane with the gamers and streamers, but it's, it's so close to all of this Other stuff that is still popping and you've just kind of got stuck on this track.
I mean it's only up until last year.
I mean it's just this year the bottom's fallen out of it.
So I guess the time is now because it's clear that it's not coming back to the same level that it was at last year for sure.
I've never seen so quick, but.
Right, yeah, this.

And that's kind of the, the gift and the curse of like gaming and live stream culture I would say, right, is that you need to be able to, to activate and mobilize audiences, content and brands very quickly.
And if you are able to be nimble, it can be very lucrative and very successful.
But the, the bottom can also fall out very quickly if you're not actively participating and engaged in, in the trends.

And I guess to your point, right in part kind of, as I mentioned earlier, seeing this, this decline, this trend downward, right From a revenue perspective, working alongside Steve and kind of projecting revenue right in 25, how we grow, maintain and sustain the business.
26, you know, we have thought and considered how we diversify the clientele.
So you know, clientele again has roots in gaming and video game content.
But a lot of the more recent content creators that we manage are creating food content and travel content.
You have gone there.
Okay, so look, clearly from where I'm sat, this business is if you carry on going the way that you've gone, you have to just get out of it.
I guess just drop it the stuff that no longer works and move on to another channel.
The influencer market is huge.
We sold an agency last year and clearly the market can change quickly.
But we sold it for 13.5 multiple of EBITDA, which is massive.
Normally agencies go for like 5x and this went for 13.
The market for great influencer agencies is still really huge.

And if anything, I think the market is predicting that influencers will become bigger and bigger and it's possibly even being fueled and one of the few industries that can be fueled by AI because influences are real and people trust them so that they are much better than any kind of other, you know, sort of general branded content because there's a high level of trust there.
And from what I'm seeing, you guys know this game, you've just done it in the gaming space.
But, and clearly you have made the move if you've got food content creators and other types of content.
But that seems to me, and that seems to me where you should go.
And I think you have the legacy to prove that you can do it for new clients as well.
So it just should be the only focus for you guys now is just doing biz dev purely in the influence of space and everybody.
Yeah, that's the pitch.
Right.
Effectively, as we go out and explore the marketplace and buyers who are still eager and invested in scaling their agency businesses and having a stronger presence and influencer.
That's exactly what I'm wanting to share.
Right.
The numbers speak for themselves.

But to your point, you know, we've been able to generate, you know, tens of millions of dollars within the influencer realm in seeing and recognizing both the emerging markets and spenders, but then also the talent that warrants that type of spend, whether it be video games, tattoos, cars, you know, it doesn't really matter.
Right.
The secret sauce is our ability to understand and pinpoint and identify where those opportunities exist.
And so we've, we've seen some of that interest come inbound, both from competitors within the gaming space that are one that have wanted to either monopolize the gaming niche.
We've also received some interest from sports management outfits, traditional Hollywood agencies that have wanted to bolster their influencer arm and marketing arm.
I just haven't found the right fit from a people perspective.
Right.
To feel like that those teams can sufficiently support both my growth, Steve's growth and the team, and a clientele's growth above and beyond what we can do independently.
And I haven't really even got into the numbers part of it with certain outfits because it just wasn't clicking.
Okay, is that your.
Is that your next move then?

Is that in your head you're thinking, unless you partner with somebody else that needs your skill set and they can kind of bolster the business while, while you find that next step, there's no point in carrying on on your own.
So the option is really quite stark.
It's like we need to find somebody that will buy in or invest or acquire the business while it's still going.
That's my focus, my priority, my intention is kind of twofold, right?
To continue to build up the value of the company by sustaining and growing the clientele.
You know, the roster size and the revenue and how we monetize, but all kind of leading up towards building the valuation for a potential acquisition.
And how far away is.
Is that?
What are you thinking?
Is it you're looking to build a backup over the next three years?
What's the time?
I mean, my ideal scenario is that we find the right partner, the right acquirer, before end of 2025 is my dream scenario.
And what kind of deal are you thinking?
What would you like to get for the business?
I. I've struggled really with really under even knowing and understanding the types of deals available.
Right.
Which is kind of why I reached out.
As confident and capable as we are, as I am in negotiation and deals and media rights, M and A is a different beast.
Right.
And so when I've entered some of these rooms and had conversations with acquirers who presented things to me, I'm out of my element.
Right.
I'm not sure what deal terms and I haven't really wanted to engage, you know, a Kirkland and Ellis or a big law firm to represent us just yet because I feel like I'm still.
You shouldn't too new, too ignorant to it and maybe just too stubborn.
Right.
I feel like maybe other folks would have just spent the money for the subject matter expert to do it.
But I'm someone that genuinely does want to learn and feel confident enough in the room, but then pass on some of the responsibility to the expert to do it alongside me.
So take your question.
I don't know the deal.
Let me just address that idea that you need to hire a big lawyer to do M and A.
That definitely isn't what you need to do that.
And if, if it does happen where you get to the point where you need a lawyer, it's right at the last minute.
You're completely right that actually it's all about chemistry.
So if you don't like them, it's not going to work out.
Even if there's tons of money on the table, it will get messy and you won't get the deal that you think you're getting in the end because you will fall out with them.
It's just the nature of how it works.
So you really do have to find somebody that you like.
But I think the issue is going to be that you guys aren't going to be happy with the offer that you could get now versus what you could have got in the middle of last year.
Because it doesn't matter at this point.
I can't lose sleep over the deals that we could have done in years past.
I need to find the right partner and outfit that sees the opportunity and value not just in what we offer today, but what we can and should be doing in subsequent years.
But I totally hear you.
I just, I know that the pandemic years and Covid times and revenue was an aberration.
And so I'm not necessarily looking to replicate that although the pitch is going to be that it's possible.
Sure.
But, you know, I'm a realist, so I can't expect anything like that to happen again.
Yeah.
To kind of piggyback off what Justin's reiterating.
It's.

Even if you look at 2023 to 2024, we did do about 7 million less in total talent sales, but the potency of our revenue continuously grew just because, you know, Justin did a great job restructuring a lot of internal contracts with our talent to either, you know, secure larger percentages of commission on our end while servicing their business as we do internally.
So, you know, there has been adjustments, there have been pivots that have been made to show that we can be savvy internally to, you know, operate this kind of business.
But yeah, echoing what Justin's saying, kind of having that, you know, that second hand to come in as that, you know, that buffer to, you know, kind of guide us is, is where.
How long do you think is left of the business?
I mean, it's kind of nosediving like that at the moment.
Are you just going to run out of clients and it's going to stop?
Or do you think that it's kind of.
It's gone as low as it will get now and it will just scoot along the bottom at two and a half million or five million a year.
Because that's not a bad business.
Not.
That's not a terrible business.
So it's not bad.
Yeah.
And.
And I think I'll say, because I know it's kind of a different answer.
Steve will have an answer that is very numerically based and talk in terms of burn rate and Runway and, and I could think about it, I think about a little bit more subjectively.
He probably has a more definitive answer.
I'll say for myself, I'm not interested in being a talent manager in the same vein, in the same workload or workflow for another seven years.

I'm wanting to ensure that myself and my team, my clientele are put into bigger, better rooms with more than just myself and my seven teammates so that their businesses can be sustainable and that I can try to transition my skill set into other avenues of entertainment and partnership and deal making.
And so I think realistically, I still have a lot of time that I want to work.
Right.
I'm 34 years old.
So realistically, I'm not looking for an exit to ride off into the sunset.
And I don't think my numbers would afford that anyways.
But at the same time, I'm willing to work as aggressively, you know, for the next three, four, five years.
Right.
With an acquirer who sees the value of my continued contribution.

If that acquisition doesn't come to fruition here by the end of the year, then the intention and goal and focus will be to continue to sign clientele, to bridge that gap of lost revenue and service them as much as possible, but spending less on the hiring and acquisition side of things.

I feel like the team that I've hired over the past three, four months is great, but I need to develop them and have them bring on more business that they can manage under our roof and kind of see if that extends our Runway and window for a potential acquisition, you know, in 26 maybe.
Okay.
So yeah, so I really needed to understand that before I could say the next bit.
Because the way that businesses are valued, obviously, and you'll know this, I'm sure, is by multiples of their ebitda.

But also it's the trajectory and a ton of other sort of factors, you know, client concentration and, you know, the quality of the contracts that you have and the type of work that you do, all of that is going to be in there.

So a buyer that comes along and looks at this business, you know, nose diving to the ground, even though it could be sustainable at this level, which is an okay business, is going to make a stupid offer.
I mean it's just going to be a low ball offer.
Now agencies of the size that you're currently at the multiples are sort of three to five times EBITDA.
And just assuming that your 315k is at your EBITDA, you know, the, the most you could get for this is 1.5.
And the way that deals are structured is they will give you half of that, maybe in cash up front and then a three year earnout.
So you're stuck in a deal with somebody and you guys are only going to take, assuming you're 50, 50, but you, you would only be taking half of that 750k each on day one.
So it's not a life changing amount at all.
You're really just looking at what can you rescue from this with like a sponsor coming in.
So if, if you guys are okay with that situation then, then, then that's fine.
And in fact it's great because the biggest problem that we have as an industry is like crazy, crazy owners thinking that their businesses are worth like 10x20x whatever.
They just see stupid numbers in the press and they think that that's what everybody gets so the reality is somebody's going to offer you a three or four times multiple.
They might offer a bit more because you've been in a sexy space.
And like I said, influencers is a growing space for sure.
So they may even put more value on it if it's a strategic acquisition.
From their point of view, it could be more than that.
But I'm just being super pessimistic because I wouldn't want to say, you know, you could get a 7x when reality never do pay more than 3 or 4 times.
But, but that seems to be the, the best route forward potentially.
And in the meantime, you guys just rebuild the business from the bottom up.
But I just wonder whether that would be special enough for you to bother handing over the business to somebody else when you could.

- JM and Steve co-founded a gaming/influencer agency 7 years ago, achieving eight-figure revenues in 2021-2022 due to the pandemic gaming boom.
- Total revenue dropped from $21M in 2023 to $14M in 2024, and only $2.5M YTD in 2025, highlighting a significant decline.

- The agency's team of 8 has a limited financial runway of 12-18 months, prompting a decision between acquisition and independent growth.
- JP seeks acquisition by the end of 2025 rather than manage the agency independently for an extended period.
- Current EBITDA is estimated at $315K, with potential adjustments leading to a valuation of 3-5x EBITDA multiple.
- Capital A Group, represented by Andy Day, specializes in M&A for marketing services and outlines a typical deal structure of 50% cash upfront and 50% earnout over 3 years.
- A website rebuild is essential for enhancing market presence and attracting potential buyers, transitioning to a more comprehensive showcase.
- Two M&A service tiers exist: $10K for basic marketplace listing and $30K for full-service engagements, with a 6-month timeline for the M&A process.
